issues.legal_issue: A conviction resting on accomplice testimony requires the accomplice to be reliable and the testimony to be corroborated in material particulars that connect the accused with the crime.
material_facts: The prosecution case depended principally on testimony from an accomplice who had participated in the events and later became an approver.
The court found the approver reliable and considered whether other evidence confirmed the part of his account implicating the accused in the crime.
issues.conclusion: An accomplice is competent to testify, but a conviction should not rest on accomplice testimony alone; after finding the accomplice reliable, the court must find reliable corroboration in material particulars connecting the accused with the crime. Corroboration must confirm the crime-implicating part of the account, not merely a collateral part.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 133 and 114 illustration (b) of the Indian Evidence Act permit accomplice testimony but embody a rule of caution against conviction on that testimony alone. Corroboration may come from another witness or from circumstances, including the accused’s conduct, and must tend to connect the accused with the crime. The court relied on Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab, [1957] S.C.R. 953, for the requirement to assess the accomplice’s reliability before considering corroboration, and Lachi Ram v. State of Punjab, [1967] 1 S.C.R. 243, for the reliability test and need for material corroboration.

predicates.proceeding_relies_on_accomplice_testimon: The prosecution in the criminal proceeding relies on testimony from a participant in the crime who has become an approver.
predicates.accomplice_found_reliable: The court finds that the approver is a reliable witness and that the account is not inherently impossible.
predicates.independent_evidence_confirms_crime_impl: Other testimony or circumstances confirm the part of the approver’s account that implicates the accused in committing the crime.

issues.definition: When a criminal proceeding relies on a reliable approver and independent evidence confirms the account implicating the accused, the approver’s evidence can support a conviction.

issues.legal_issue: Circumstantial evidence concerning the victim’s last company, the disposal of stolen property, and the close connection between a murder and theft can sufficiently corroborate an approver’s account against accused persons involved in the same transaction.
material_facts: Witnesses saw the deceased with the approver and one accused shortly before the death; the deceased’s clothing was also identified in evidence associated with the body.
Articles taken from the grandfather’s house were traced to the son through production, pledging, sale, or recovery, and the son was connected with the disposal of several items.
The father was connected with articles from the house that were sold or given to another person, and he was associated with his son in the disposal of property, including a cycle carrier.
The father and son were closely associated in disposing of the stolen articles, and the murder and theft occurred in close proximity and were found to form one transaction.
issues.conclusion: The evidence provided sufficient corroboration in material particulars of the approver’s account and established the accused persons’ guilt of the offences charged; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Applying sections 133 and 114 illustration (b) of the Indian Evidence Act and the principles in Sarwan Singh v. State of Punjab, [1957] S.C.R. 953, and Lachi Ram v. State of Punjab, [1967] 1 S.C.R. 243, the court held that corroboration need not independently prove the actual killing if the evidence, considered together, confirms the approver’s crime-implicating account. Circumstantial evidence, including conduct and the handling of stolen property, can connect an accused to the crime. The close temporal and factual connection between the murder and theft supported treating them as one composite transaction.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal involving a reliable approver, the victim’s presence with an accused and the approver before death, the tracing and joint disposal of stolen property, and the finding that the murder and theft were one transaction can together sufficiently corroborate the approver to support convictions.
